content: Ultrasound is a diagnostic imaging technique that utilizes high-frequency sound waves to create images of structures within the body. In the context of early pregnancy, it is commonly employed to assess the developing fetus. During early pregnancy, ultrasound is used to confirm the presence of an intrauterine pregnancy and to exclude ectopic pregnancy, which occurs when the fertilized egg implants outside the uterus. It is also utilized to determine the gestational age of the pregnancy by measuring the crown-rump length (CRL) of the embryo, which is considered the most accurate method for dating in the first trimester. Ultrasound can identify the presence of a yolk sac, which is an early structure that provides nutrients to the developing embryo. The visualization of a yolk sac is a reassuring sign of a viable pregnancy. Additionally, the detection of fetal cardiac activity, typically visible by transvaginal ultrasound around 5.5 to 6 weeks of gestation, is a critical indicator of embryonic viability. This imaging modality is also used to evaluate the number of gestational sacs and embryos, which is essential for diagnosing multiple pregnancies, such as twins or higher-order multiples. Furthermore, it can help identify abnormalities in the gestational sac, such as irregular shape or absence of a yolk sac, which may suggest a non-viable pregnancy or an impending miscarriage. Ultrasound in early pregnancy is also instrumental in assessing the uterus and adnexa (the structures adjacent to the uterus, including the ovaries and fallopian tubes). This evaluation can help detect uterine anomalies, fibroids, or ovarian cysts that may impact the pregnancy. In cases of vaginal bleeding or pelvic pain during early pregnancy, ultrasound is a critical tool for determining the cause, such as subchorionic hemorrhage, miscarriage, or ectopic pregnancy. It provides valuable information to guide clinical management and ensure the best possible outcomes for both the patient and the developing fetus.
